reason: The Book of Esther does not present a narrative where regular people are portrayed as being in the wrong while their leaders are in the right. Rather, the story features: (1) the Jewish people as innocent victims facing annihilation through no fault of their own; (2) Haman, a leader figure, as the villain whose evil plot is thwarted; (3) Esther and Mordecai as protagonists who, while holding some official positions, are portrayed as courageous and morally right in their actions; and (4) King Ahasuerus as a somewhat foolish, easily manipulated figure who is not presented as particularly wise or right in his judgments. The central conflict is not between leaders being right and common people being wrong, but rather between good individuals (Esther, Mordecai, the Jewish people) defending themselves against an evil plot by a leader (Haman). The Jews' refusal to bow to Haman and their self-defense are presented as justified, not as wrongdoing.
